Everything about a bundle is fixed except its passphrase, which makes the
passphrase the only part a person decides and the only part an attacker can
work on. Ask someone for one and you get one they thought up, drawn from a far
smaller set than it looks. `pack` stops asking.

### Changed

- `pack` draws 24 random characters and puts them on the clipboard.

  ```sh
  monkeys pack
  ```
  > ```
  > wrote /tmp/a.monsecrets: +foo @test,production @production, 5 secrets
  > copied its passphrase to your clipboard; send that the other way
  > ```

  They are never printed, so nothing lands in a terminal's scrollback, a CI log
  or an agent's transcript beside the path of the file they open. That is the
  rule the whole tool keeps and the reason there is no `get`. The characters are
  drawn uniformly from 62 with the high bytes rejected, because 256 is not a
  multiple of 62 and folding them would favour the front of the alphabet.

### Added

- `pack --ask` prompts for a passphrase you choose and leaves the clipboard
  alone. A machine with no clipboard tool says so and asks, since a file whose
  passphrase nobody has is a file nobody can open, and a passphrase piped in
  still works for the scripts that do that.

### Documentation

- [How it works](https://docs.monk3ys.dev/docs/how-it-works/): the three places
  a name or a secret can be, what each command moves between them, and what
  `run` does with a fork.
- The advice for a bundle committed by mistake said to delete it and change the
  passphrase. Changing it does nothing: the copy that leaked is sealed with the
  old one and stays readable by whoever guesses that. Rotate the secrets inside,
  the way any secret that has been somewhere it should not be is rotated.
